info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 5.1: Double-Keying and Building a Consensus Text.

name.text: 01 Question: Why the Ground Truth Needs Verifying

questiontext.text: Why is a single-pass manual diplomatic transcription insufficient to serve as an unverified ground truth reference?

generalfeedback.text: Two independent passes rarely err identically, so disagreement between them localizes error precisely.

answer.text: Single-pass transcription inevitably contains errors, which cause correct machine readings to be mis-scored as errors and fine-tuned models to learn flawed patterns.

feedback.text: Correct. Flawed ground truth silently inflates measured error rates, propagates mistakes into trained models, and biases subsequent adjudication toward the reference's errors.

answer.text: Single-pass transcription fails schema validation because human editors cannot manually format TEI XML elements correctly.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structural validity is a property of the XML schema and validation toolchain, not the reason why textual characters require verification.

answer.text: Optical character recognition engines reject training sets that have not been certified by an external institutional body.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Training pipelines accept any text input regardless of certification; the problem is statistical error propagation, not software rejection.

answer.text: Single-pass transcription takes twice as long as double-keying because transcribers pause to deliberate on every ambiguous letterform.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Double-keying takes roughly twice as long as a single pass; single-pass transcription is faster but prone to uncorrected errors.

questiontext.text: What character accuracy threshold is typically required by formal guidelines like the German Research Foundation (DFG) for virtually error-free digitization?

generalfeedback.text: Double-keying reaches 99.95% or better on printed text; a single manuscript pass is well below that, which is why today is required.

answer.text: 99.997%, representing no more than 3 errors per 100,000 characters.

feedback.text: Correct. The DFG guidelines set 99.997% (3 errors per 100k characters) as the standard for high-accuracy digital corpora.

answer.text: 95.0%, representing roughly 5 errors per 100 characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A 95% accuracy level (5% CER) is marginal for commercial entry and far below scholarly digitization standards.

answer.text: 99.0%, representing roughly 10 errors per 1,000 characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. 99.0% (1% CER) is common for raw OCR baselines, but professional double-keying targets 99.95% or higher.

answer.text: 100.0%, representing absolute perfection across all morphological forms without exception.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Absolute 100% accuracy is statistically unattainable at scale; guidelines define specific fractional tolerances like 99.997%.

questiontext.text: Why did the Deutsches Textarchiv deliberately employ transcribers who did not understand German for its double-keying workflow?

generalfeedback.text: Professional double-keying uses transcribers who cannot read the language, because comprehension causes auto-correction — so do not reread your first pass.

answer.text: Severing semantic comprehension from grapheme recognition neutralizes psychological auto-correction, preventing transcribers from silently modernizing historical spellings or supplying missing letters.

feedback.text: Correct. When transcribers cannot read the language for meaning, they transcribe strictly what they see rather than what they cognitively expect.

answer.text: Non-native speakers were legally required by funding agreements governing pan-European digital infrastructure projects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The choice was methodological and psychological, not a legal mandate.

answer.text: Transcribers with linguistic expertise refused to follow strict double-keying key stroke capture protocols.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The reason is cognitive auto-correction, not insubordination by subject specialists.

answer.text: Non-native speakers type significantly faster because they do not pause to look up grammatical paradigms in historical lexicons.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Speed was not the driving factor; preventing cognitive normalization of historical orthography was.

questiontext.text: How do typographical errors differ fundamentally from structural errors in TEI transcription?

generalfeedback.text: Double-keying finds character errors and cannot find structural ones — perfect characters in wrong markup still misrepresent the document.

answer.text: Typographical errors occur in the character stream and are detected by character-level comparisons, whereas structural errors occur in the markup architecture and require schema or Schematron validation.

feedback.text: Correct. Double-keying character comparisons detect typographical slips (omissions, substitutions), but cannot detect structural markup misidentifications such as glosses tagged as body text.

answer.text: Typographical errors invalidate the XML document object model, whereas structural errors only affect visual font rendering.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Structural errors (e.g. unclosed tags or invalid nesting) compromise the XML document model; typographical errors affect the string contents.

answer.text: Typographical errors can be identified only by human peer review, whereas structural errors are automatically corrected by HTR decoders.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Typographical differences are readily found by computational string comparison; structural errors require schema validation and human architectural review.

answer.text: Typographical errors affect only modern print transcriptions, whereas structural errors are unique to handwritten medieval codices.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Both classes of error occur across all digital transcription projects regardless of the physical medium.

questiontext.text: Why is it essential to commit your second transcription pass to version control before comparing it with the first pass?

generalfeedback.text: Commit the second pass before comparing, so that its independence is verifiable in the history rather than merely asserted.

answer.text: Committing before comparison creates an immutable cryptographic record in Git that proves the second pass was produced independently without prior bias.

feedback.text: Correct. If comparison occurs before committing, the second pass can be silently altered, destroying the verifiable claim of independent replication.

answer.text: Git refuses to run diff algorithms between files that have not both been committed to the repository index.

feedback.text: Incorrect. `git diff --no-index` can compare any arbitrary uncommitted files on disk; the requirement is methodological and evidentiary.

answer.text: Committing the second pass automatically merges the two XML trees into a single consensus draft.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git commit simply snapshots the state; reconciliation requires deliberate manual adjudication.

answer.text: The TEI schema validation engine will reject XML files that do not carry a commit hash in their header metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI schemas validate XML grammar, not Git commit metadata.

questiontext.text: Why must both transcription passes be normalized to Unicode NFC prior to computational comparison?

generalfeedback.text: Normalize to NFC before comparing, or every accented character reports as a difference — and check line counts before anything else.

answer.text: Without NFC normalization, identical characters encoded in composed versus decomposed forms will report false-positive differences at every accented letter.

feedback.text: Correct. Polytonic Greek can represent the same accented vowel as a single precomposed code point (NFC) or a base letter plus combining diacritics (NFD); normalization ensures identical storage.

answer.text: NFC normalization strips all polytonic accents and breathings, reducing Greek text to monotonic ASCII.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NFC preserves all polytonic diacritics in their canonical precomposed forms; it does not strip them.

answer.text: Computational diff tools can operate only on Latin-1 encodings and fail on multi-byte UTF-8 without conversion.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Modern diff utilities handle UTF-8 seamlessly; NFC resolves character decomposition variances, not 8-bit character sets.

answer.text: NFC normalization automatically aligns line numbers between files with unequal line break counts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. NFC operates on Unicode strings; it has no effect on line counts or document alignment.

questiontext.text: When adjudicating a disagreement between your two transcription passes, what is the proper methodological procedure?

generalfeedback.text: Adjudicate by looking at the ink, not by choosing the reading that makes better sense — that is the error the method exists to neutralize.

answer.text: Inspect the manuscript facsimile at full zoom to verify the physical ink, resisting the temptation to select whichever reading seems more contextually plausible.

feedback.text: Correct. Selecting the reading that makes better sense re-introduces the psychological auto-correction bias the double-keying method was designed to eliminate.

answer.text: Always default to the first pass because it was produced before transcriber fatigue set in.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Pass 1 is just as fallible as pass 2, and pass 2 benefits from greater familiarity with the hand; only the physical ink decides.

answer.text: Adopt whichever reading appears in modern standard critical print editions of the text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic transcription records the unique witness on the page, not the eclectically reconstructed text of modern print editions.

answer.text: Automatically discard both readings and replace them with an editorial conjecture.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Editorial conjecture belongs to eclectic edition building, not diplomatic transcription of manuscript evidence.

questiontext.text: How should genuine, unresolvable palaeographical ambiguities between the two passes be recorded in the consensus XML?

generalfeedback.text: Keep both passes alongside the consensus — the passes are the evidence for how the consensus was reached.

answer.text: Encode the ambiguity using <choice> and multiple <unclear> elements with candidate readings, preserving the evidential uncertainty.

feedback.text: Correct. Recording unresolved readings with `` and `` honestly documents the manuscript's physical state without discarding evidence.

answer.text: Delete the ambiguous word entirely from the text and record it only in an external private spreadsheet.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting the text destroys diplomatic completeness; TEI provides explicit elements like `` and `` for this purpose.

answer.text: Pick one reading arbitrarily and append a comment forbidding future editors from revisiting the line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Arbitrary choices conceal uncertainty; digital editions aim for transparent, revisable evidential records.

answer.text: Force the XML parser to halt compilation until a second expert palaeographer adjudicates the line.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unresolvable readings are normal in historical documents and must be formally encoded within the TEI structure.

questiontext.text: Why is Krippendorff's alpha preferred over simple percentage agreement and Cohen's kappa for evaluating transcription agreement?

generalfeedback.text: Percentage agreement ignores chance; use a chance-adjusted metric, and prefer Krippendorff's alpha because it handles missing data.

answer.text: Krippendorff's alpha corrects for chance agreement, accommodates missing data, and supports any number of raters across multiple data types.

feedback.text: Correct. Percentage agreement ignores chance matching, and Cohen's kappa is restricted to exactly two raters and suffers from paradoxes on skewed category distributions.

answer.text: Krippendorff's alpha is the only metric supported natively by Git's internal merge engine.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git merge algorithms do not use statistical inter-rater agreement metrics.

answer.text: Percentage agreement cannot be computed on strings longer than 256 characters.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Percentage agreement is simple to compute at any length; its flaw is theoretical (ignoring chance agreement).

answer.text: Cohen's kappa requires all transcription files to be formatted as binary SQLite databases.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Cohen's kappa is a mathematical formula for categorical ratings, completely independent of database formats.

name.text: 10 Question: Computing Agreement on Your Passes

questiontext.text: When analyzing per-line character agreement between your two passes, what does a sudden collapse in agreement from line 12 onward typically indicate?

generalfeedback.text: Report the distribution of agreement, not just the mean — a sudden collapse means line skip, not difficulty.

answer.text: A line skip or missing line break occurred in one pass, misaligning all subsequent lines.

feedback.text: Correct. A sharp drop in agreement that persists across subsequent lines is classic evidence of a structural line skip, which must be realigned before evaluating character error.

answer.text: The scribe abruptly switched languages from Greek to Latin halfway down the folio.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Language shifts in a single text column are rare; misalignment from an omitted line is the standard cause.

answer.text: The Unicode consortium updated the code point definitions mid-document.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unicode standards are fixed; software encoding does not mutate across lines.

answer.text: The transcriber's monitor resolution automatically downscaled during transcription.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Hardware display settings do not alter character strings in text files.

name.text: 11 Question: Case Study: The Deutsches Textarchiv

questiontext.text: Why did the Deutsches Textarchiv (DTA) choose to bypass OCR entirely for its foundational corpus of 1600–1900 German texts?

generalfeedback.text: The DTA rejected OCR for difficult typography and normalized only after reconciliation — a separate layer over a verified diplomatic base.

answer.text: Manual double-keying was economically superior to correcting the high error rates generated by OCR on early modern Fraktur and irregular orthography.

feedback.text: Correct. When recognition error rates exceed economic thresholds, manual double-keying costs less in labor and time than exhaustive post-correction of noisy OCR.

answer.text: German copyright law in 2013 prohibited the application of automated machine learning algorithms to printed books.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The decision was driven by accuracy and post-correction economics, not intellectual property restrictions.

answer.text: OCR software was unable to output Unicode UTF-8 character encodings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Commercial OCR engines supported UTF-8; the problem was severe graphemic misrecognition on historical Fraktur fonts.

answer.text: The DTA intended to prevent modern researchers from conducting full-text keyword searches.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The DTA's ultimate goal was high-precision linguistic search, which demanded virtually error-free double-keyed text.

name.text: 12 Question: Structure and the Base Format

questiontext.text: Why did the DTA establish the DTA Base Format (DTABf) as a strict, constrained subset of TEI P5?

generalfeedback.text: TEI permits several valid encodings of the same feature, so consistency requires an explicit convention — your CONVENTIONS.md is that document.

answer.text: Full TEI P5 is deliberately permissive and allows multiple valid ways to encode the same phenomenon, which creates fatal inconsistencies across large collaborative corpora.

feedback.text: Correct. Constraining the markup schema ensures that structural elements (such as marginal notes or speaker tags) are encoded identically across thousands of texts.

answer.text: Full TEI P5 is proprietary commercial software requiring expensive annual site licenses.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI P5 is an open-source, community-governed standard.

answer.text: DTABf replaced XML syntax with JSON-LD to optimize web browser rendering speeds.

feedback.text: Incorrect. DTABf is an XML TEI schema subset, not a JSON format.

answer.text: The TEI Consortium deprecated all manuscript elements in the official P5 release.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI P5 includes extensive manuscript modules; DTABf constrained them for consistency.

questiontext.text: If a tag frequency audit reveals six <unclear> elements in pass 1 but only two in pass 2, what does this discrepancy primarily indicate?

generalfeedback.text: Differing counts signal an inconsistent threshold, not a disagreement about the text — fix the convention, not the instances.

answer.text: An inconsistent subjective threshold for uncertainty between the two sessions, which should be resolved by defining clear criteria in CONVENTIONS.md.

feedback.text: Correct. Varying counts of interpretive tags reflect subjective threshold drift rather than raw textual disagreement; formalizing the rule resolves the inconsistency.

answer.text: The first pass was corrupted by an invalid XML entity parser.

feedback.text: Incorrect. A difference in valid tag counts indicates varying human editorial judgement, not file corruption.

answer.text: The manuscript facsimile lost resolution while the second pass was being transcribed.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The image remains constant; the transcriber's subjective certainty threshold shifted.

answer.text: TEI schemas automatically delete <unclear> tags when character confidence exceeds 80%.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schemas do not alter file contents or evaluate confidence levels dynamically.

name.text: 14 Question: Consensus Without a Second Person

questiontext.text: What is the primary methodological vulnerability of self-double-keying (performing both passes yourself)?

generalfeedback.text: Self double-keying cannot catch your systematic misunderstandings — exchange lines with a classmate, and examine points where the machine disagrees with both passes.

answer.text: Correlated error: you are likely to repeat your own systematic palaeographical misunderstandings and blind spots identically in both passes.

feedback.text: Correct. When both passes are produced by the same individual, systematic misreadings produce false agreement, allowing errors to slip through undetected.

answer.text: Git cannot track multiple commits authored by the same user email address.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git effortlessly records unlimited commits from the same author.

answer.text: Single-author double-keying violates the TEI P5 abstract syntax specification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI markup rules govern XML document structure, not how many humans transcribed the source.

answer.text: Self-double-keying produces incompatible normalization forms in alternating passes.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Normalization form is controlled by editor configuration and software tools, not author identity.

name.text: 15 Question: Where Human and Machine Errors Differ

questiontext.text: How do error topologies typically differ between human transcribers and statistical language/recognition models?

generalfeedback.text: Humans transcribe what they see even when it makes no sense; models transcribe what they expect — which is why unique forms are exactly where models fail.

answer.text: Humans transcribe what they see even when it is meaningless, whereas models transcribe what they statistically expect, frequently replacing unfamiliar forms with high-probability words.

feedback.text: Correct. Humans make cognitive letter substitutions but preserve oddities, while language models hallucinate plausible words, expand abbreviations unprompted, and suffer out-of-vocabulary failures.

answer.text: Humans make errors primarily at line boundaries, whereas models make errors exclusively in the center of words.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models struggle heavily with line-boundary fractures and hyphenation; humans understand word continuations naturally.

answer.text: Models never make character substitution errors, failing only on full-paragraph deletions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models frequently commit character insertions, deletions, and substitutions along with structural failures.

answer.text: Human errors are entirely predictable by mathematical formulas, whereas machine errors are completely random.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Machine error distributions reflect statistical training weights and token probabilities, which can be systematically analyzed.

name.text: 16 Question: Line-End Hyphenation and CTC Alignment

questiontext.text: What notable finding emerged from the Bullinger dataset research regarding CTC alignment of continuous expert transcriptions to line images?

generalfeedback.text: Consensus means reconciling text with the page's physical coordinates, not only correcting characters — which is why line alignment is checked first.

answer.text: Alignment accuracy was often higher using a weakly trained HTR model than an overfitted model, because the weaker model had not learned to reproduce broken hyphenation errors.

feedback.text: Correct. Peer et al. (2025) demonstrated that over-optimized models learned the layout flaws of the training data, whereas weaker models aligned continuous text more flexibly.

answer.text: CTC alignment eliminated the need for dynamic programming matrices in sequence alignment.

feedback.text: Incorrect. CTC alignment relies directly on dynamic programming over character posterior probabilities.

answer.text: Latin and premodern German letters cannot be aligned to bounding boxes without vector SVG fonts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Alignment operates on pixel coordinates and line polygons, not vector font outlines.

answer.text: Line-end hyphenation in 16th-century texts was completely standardized and required no algorithmic handling.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical texts exhibit highly irregular hyphenation and layout splits across lines.

name.text: 17 Question: Consensus as a Living Document

questiontext.text: How did the Australian Newspaper Digitisation Program (Trove) cost-effectively manage OCR quality across vast historical archives?

generalfeedback.text: A published edition can be a living document that improves through recorded correction, rather than a text claiming finality.

answer.text: Contractors guaranteed high accuracy on structural metadata and the first four lines, while exposing raw OCR for the remaining body text to decentralized public correction.

feedback.text: Correct. Trove adopted a living-document model where critical navigational metadata was verified upfront while crowdsourcing long-tail body text corrections over time.

answer.text: They discarded all OCR and required users to read only raw raster TIFF scans.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Trove made raw OCR searchable and interactive, enabling keyword discovery and crowd correction.

answer.text: They banned volunteers from correcting text to protect academic copyright.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Public volunteer text correction was the core innovation of the Trove platform.

answer.text: They used ROVER voting exclusively without human verification of any metadata.

feedback.text: Incorrect. High-value metadata (titles, subtitles, opening lines) received rigorous manual verification to 99.5% accuracy.

name.text: 18 Question: ROVER and Your Three Transcriptions

questiontext.text: How can Recognizer Output Voting for Error Reduction (ROVER) logic be productively applied when comparing human and machine transcriptions?

generalfeedback.text: Where both machines agree against both your passes, look again — their errors are uncorrelated with yours, so their agreement is a real signal.

answer.text: Points where both HTR and VLM models agree with each other but disagree with both human passes serve as high-priority flags to re-examine the physical ink for human expectation error.

feedback.text: Correct. Machine error distributions are uncorrelated with human cognitive biases; when two distinct models agree against human passes, the human transcriber may have misread the ink.

answer.text: Taking a simple mathematical majority vote across two machine outputs and two human passes automatically yields the true text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Simple majority voting across unequal hypotheses inappropriately equates noisy machine guesses with verified human readings.

answer.text: ROVER should be used to automatically overwrite all human diplomatic tags with modern monotonic spellings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ROVER is a sequence alignment and voting algorithm, not an orthographic modernizer.

answer.text: Machine transcriptions should always be discarded if they disagree with even a single unverified human reading.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Machine disagreement often reveals human slips, making uncorrelated machine outputs valuable diagnostic flags.

questiontext.text: What constitutes a scholarly, assessable reconciliation record in logs/reconciliation-w5.md?

generalfeedback.text: Record each disagreement with both readings, the adjudication, and the reason — that record is the assignment and the seed of your commentary.

answer.text: Documenting each disagreement with its exact line number, both candidate readings, the adjudicated outcome, and the specific palaeographical rationale.

feedback.text: Correct. Scholarly auditing requires full evidential transparency for every decision rather than opaque summary statements like 'fixed line 14'.

answer.text: Listing only the total count of resolved lines without preserving the rejected candidate readings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Omitting candidate readings destroys the audit trail needed to evaluate how decisions were made.

answer.text: Pasting the raw Python script output without human commentary or palaeographical explanation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Raw diffs show differences but fail to record editorial reasoning and physical ink verification.

answer.text: Summarizing all discrepancies as 'minor typographical adjustments' without line-by-line attribution.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Vague summaries fail assignment assessment standards and provide no basis for future commentary.

questiontext.text: Why must the original ground truth tag (gt-f42r) be preserved when tagging the new consensus text (gt-f42r-consensus)?

generalfeedback.text: Tag the consensus but keep the original ground truth tag — the difference between measurements against each shows how much error was yours.

answer.text: Retaining the original tag ensures that Week 4's baseline measurements remain fully reproducible and allows editors to calculate how much error was in the human reference.

feedback.text: Correct. Overwriting or deleting the historical tag makes prior research reports irreproducible and hides the measurement of human reference error.

answer.text: Git repositories will become corrupted if an existing tag object is referenced by subsequent commits.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git tags are lightweight or annotated pointers; retaining multiple tags is standard and safe.

answer.text: The TEI header requires two distinct Git commit hashes to pass RelaxNG validation.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Schema validation does not check Git repository tag objects.

answer.text: Remote servers automatically reject pushes that contain fewer than three simultaneous ground truth tags.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git remotes accept any valid refspec pushed by the user.

name.text: 21 Question: How Much Did the Ground Truth Change?

questiontext.text: What is the methodological significance of measuring the Character Error Rate of pass 1 against your final consensus text?

generalfeedback.text: Measure pass 1 against the consensus — that number states how much of Week 4's measured machine error was actually yours.

answer.text: It quantifies the exact error rate of your initial baseline, revealing how much of Week 4's measured 'machine error' was actually human reference error.

feedback.text: Correct. Measuring pass 1 against consensus converts vague assumptions of human imperfection into a precise, reportable metric of baseline reliability.

answer.text: It proves that manual transcription is inherently unsuited for historical document processing.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Measuring reference error demonstrates the value of calibration, not the abandonment of human expertise.

answer.text: It determines whether the XML file needs to be converted into an external relational database.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Baseline CER evaluation is an audit metric, entirely unrelated to database architecture.

answer.text: It calculates the licensing fee owed to the repository holding the manuscript.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Error rate calculations assess transcription fidelity, not copyright or licensing terms.

questiontext.text: What critical structural condition must be met across all human and machine transcriptions before Friday's error benchmarking can proceed?

generalfeedback.text: Ensure all outputs are line-aligned and all tags are pushed — Friday's measurement retrieves tagged states and needs line alignment.

answer.text: All transcriptions must be line-aligned to ensure that character and word error rates correspond to matching line segments on the manuscript.

feedback.text: Correct. If an automated pass reflowed text or skipped a line, character calculations become unaligned, corrupting line-by-line and aggregate metrics.

answer.text: All transcriptions must be translated into modern idiomatic English prose.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Error rate benchmarking measures diplomatic fidelity to the Greek source, not English translation.

answer.text: Every XML tag must be stripped permanently from the Git repository history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Tags in the repository preserve history; preprocessing scripts strip markup in memory during measurement.

answer.text: All files must be encrypted with GPG signatures before the script can execute.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Local evaluation scripts require standard readable text files, not cryptographic encryption.

name.text: 23 Question: A Note on Today's Date

questiontext.text: In the context of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, how do digital humanities scholars reflect on the broader implications of preservation technologies?

generalfeedback.text: The week's technical sense of 'reconciliation' is unrelated to the national day; the coincidence is a reasonable moment to notice whose documents digitization has prioritized.

answer.text: They recognize that digitization funding, cataloging standards, and machine learning corpora reflect historical power dynamics that prioritized certain archives and languages over others.

feedback.text: Correct. The specialization gap in machine models highlights how historical investment has favored select cultural traditions while leaving others under-resourced.

answer.text: They mandate that all historical Greek manuscripts be removed from open-access digital repositories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Scholarly reflection promotes equitable access and critical awareness, not the suppression of open collections.

answer.text: They assert that computational transcription algorithms are completely objective and free from cultural bias.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Models reflect the biases and imbalances of the datasets used to train them.

answer.text: They replace all manuscript sigla with alphabetical identifiers assigned by federal regulatory agencies.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Manuscript sigla follow philological conventions; reflection concerns structural resource allocation in cultural heritage.

questiontext.text: Why does leaving a second pass unfinished fundamentally block Friday's measurement session?

generalfeedback.text: Friday measures against the consensus, so an unfinished second pass blocks the session.

answer.text: Without a completed second pass and adjudicated consensus text, there is no calibrated reference against which machine outputs can be legitimately benchmarked.

feedback.text: Correct. Benchmarking requires a verified ground truth; measuring against an unverified single pass perpetuates uncalibrated baseline errors.

answer.text: The Git server will automatically lock the repository against further commits after 24 hours of inactivity.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Git places no time limits on commit activity.

answer.text: The Python compiler will refuse to execute edit distance algorithms on single-author repositories.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Edit distance scripts execute on any provided string inputs regardless of completion status.

answer.text: TEI schemas require daily timestamp validation to prevent XML decay.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XML files and schemas are static text files that do not decay or expire.

questiontext.text: If a student runs a computational comparison between two transcription passes and finds almost zero differences across an entire folio of difficult Greek minuscule, what is the most probable explanation?

generalfeedback.text: Near-identical passes usually mean the second was not independent — genuine independence produces genuine disagreement.

answer.text: The second pass was not truly independent, having been copied from or heavily influenced by memory of the first pass.

feedback.text: Correct. Genuine independent transcription of complex medieval handwriting inevitably produces discrepancies; near-zero differences indicate a lack of independence.

answer.text: The student has achieved flawless palaeographical mastery surpassing institutional benchmarks.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Even expert palaeographers exhibit minor variations; zero differences in student work strongly suggests biased proofreading rather than independent double-keying.

answer.text: The Greek minuscule hand was printed using 15th-century moveable metal type.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The manuscript is a handwritten codex, not a printed edition.

answer.text: The diff utility automatically suppressed all character discrepancies below a 5% significance threshold.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Standard diff utilities report every binary or character mismatch with absolute fidelity.

name.text: 26 Question: What Good Work Looks Like Here

questiontext.text: What distinguishes an exemplary, rigorous reconciliation audit from a minimally acceptable submission?

generalfeedback.text: Reporting how wrong your own ground truth was is what makes your other figures trustworthy.

answer.text: Transparently reporting the measured error rate of the initial ground truth baseline and documenting the palaeographical rationale for all adjudications.

feedback.text: Correct. High-quality scholarly work openly acknowledges the fallibility of its reference and provides clear, evidence-based rationales for every editorial decision.

answer.text: Claiming 100% perfection across all passes and omitting any mention of unresolved readings.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Claiming perfection conceals evidential reality; scholarship values honest documentation of uncertainty.

answer.text: Generating automated XML markup using external AI APIs without human verification.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unverified AI generation violates the core requirement of human-verified diplomatic grounding.

answer.text: Deleting all intermediate Git commits to present a pristine, linear repository history.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Deleting commits destroys the audit trail that demonstrates how the consensus was achieved.

name.text: 27 Question: The Epistemology of the Consensus Text

questiontext.text: In digital textual scholarship, how should the status of a 'consensus text' be epistemologically understood?

generalfeedback.text: The consensus text is the current state of an argument, not the true text — and the version history is what lets it be corrected without loss.

answer.text: As a provisional, well-supported hypothesis representing the current state of an argument, which remains open to revision as further understanding of the hand develops.

feedback.text: Correct. A consensus text is not an infallible absolute; version control enables transparent revision without discarding the history of how earlier readings were reached.

answer.text: As an immutable, permanently settled monument that can never be altered by future scholarship.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Textual scholarship treats all editions as revisable hypotheses subject to new evidence.

answer.text: As an eclectic text reconstructed to reflect the lost original authorial autograph.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Diplomatic consensus reconstructs the reading of a specific physical manuscript witness, not an idealized authorial archetype.

answer.text: As a purely synthetic string generated by statistical majority voting without human accountability.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The consensus is established through human adjudication against physical evidence.

questiontext.text: When expanding a project beyond a single folio where full double-keying of all pages is cost-prohibitive, what is the recommended methodology?

generalfeedback.text: Stratify verification by stakes and state which parts received which treatment — uniform presentation of non-uniform work is the failure.

answer.text: Apply stratified verification: perform full double-keying on training, measurement, and variant-rich folios, while using single-pass correction on clean sections, and explicitly state this stratification in the editorial declaration.

feedback.text: Correct. Stratified verification allocates rigorous double-keying to high-stakes zones while maintaining full transparency regarding which treatment each section received.

answer.text: Secretly use automated OCR on the remaining folios while claiming uniform double-keying across the entire work.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Misrepresenting automated output as double-keyed text is a fatal breach of scholarly ethics.

answer.text: Abandon ground truth verification entirely and publish raw machine transcriptions without review.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Unverified machine output lacks diplomatic reliability and corrupts downstream research.

answer.text: Limit the edition strictly to 24 lines and refuse to transcribe the remainder of the manuscript.

generalfeedback.text: Week 6 normalizes over the consensus text — and normalizing before reconciling would entangle regularizations with corrections irrecoverably.

answer.text: Normalizing an unverified transcription entangles transcription errors with editorial regularizations, making it impossible for future readers to distinguish manuscript readings from editorial fixes.

feedback.text: Correct. Establishing a clean diplomatic consensus first ensures that normalization operates as a distinct, traceable layer over verified manuscript evidence.

questiontext.text: In the overarching structure of the course, what role did double-keying play in relation to Week 4's transcription work?

generalfeedback.text: An uncalibrated ground truth produces measurements that look precise and are not — double-keying calibrates it, and the amount of correction is itself a reportable figure.

answer.text: It calibrated the measuring instrument: verifying the baseline reference ensures that subsequent benchmarks measure actual machine performance rather than human reference errors.

feedback.text: Correct. An uncalibrated ground truth distorts all downstream error measurements; double-keying ensures the measuring standard itself is statistically reliable.

answer.text: It replaced all manual transcription with fully autonomous neural network pipelines.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Double-keying is an intensive human verification protocol, not an autonomous neural pipeline.

answer.text: It eliminated the need to record provenance metadata in Git commit trailers.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Provenance trailers remain essential for tracking human versus machine contributions across all stages.

answer.text: It proved that character error rates are completely independent of training data quality.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Training data quality directly dictates model performance; calibrating ground truth is vital for both training and evaluation.
